missing_spec_content.spec_text: The weight of an object may be considered to act at a single point referred to as the object’s ‘centre of mass’.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson never mentions centre of mass.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: The weight of an object and the mass of an object are directly proportional.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson gives W = mg but never states that weight is directly proportional to mass. It also never introduces the ∝ symbol (MS 3a).

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Weight is measured using a calibrated spring-balance (a newtonmeter).
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson does not say how weight is measured.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: The force of gravity close to the Earth is due to the gravitational field around the Earth.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson defines weight as the force of gravity but never links it to the Earth's gravitational field.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: (HT only) A single force can be resolved into two components acting at right angles to each other. The two component forces together have the same effect as the single force.
missing_spec_content.why: Resolving forces into components is not taught.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: (HT only) Students should be able to use vector diagrams to illustrate resolution of forces, equilibrium situations and determine the resultant of two forces, to include both magnitude and direction (scale drawings only).
missing_spec_content.why: Vector diagrams and scale drawings are not covered. The lesson only adds and subtracts forces acting in a straight line.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: (HT only) describe examples of the forces acting on an isolated object or system
missing_spec_content.why: Free body diagrams are described, but the lesson does not cover describing the forces on an isolated object or system.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: The acceleration of an object is proportional to the resultant force acting on the object, and inversely proportional to the mass of the object.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson only says 'more force → more acceleration; more mass → less acceleration'. It never states the proportional and inversely proportional relationships.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: (HT only) ... inertial mass is defined as the ratio of force over acceleration.
missing_spec_content.why: Inertial mass is described only as 'the mass measured by F = ma'. The lesson never defines it explicitly as the ratio F/a.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to estimate the speed, accelerations and forces involved in large accelerations for everyday road transport. Students should recognise and be able to use the symbol that indicates an approximate value or approximate answer, ~
missing_spec_content.why: Estimation for road transport and the ~ symbol are not covered.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Required practical activity 7: investigate the effect of varying the force on the acceleration of an object of constant mass, and the effect of varying the mass of an object on the acceleration produced by a constant force.
missing_spec_content.why: The required practical is not mentioned.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to apply Newton’s Third Law to examples of equilibrium situations.
missing_spec_content.why: None of the Third Law examples (wall, rocket, Earth–person) is analysed as an equilibrium situation. The book-on-table equilibrium appears only under the First Law. The lesson never explains that weight and the normal reaction force on the book are not a Third Law pair.

above_gcse.text: Experiments show that inertial mass equals gravitational mass (the mass in W = mg). This holds to extremely high precision.
above_gcse.why: The specification does not require the equivalence of inertial and gravitational mass. It could confuse students about what inertial mass means.

above_gcse.text: Mass measured by resistance to acceleration using F = ma; equal to gravitational mass
above_gcse.why: Same issue: the specification does not require the equivalence of inertial and gravitational mass.

above_gcse.text: Inertial mass — measured from F = ma; equals gravitational mass in all experiments
above_gcse.why: Same issue: the specification does not require the equivalence of inertial and gravitational mass.

factual_errors.text: Friction and air resistance are the resultant forces that slow real objects.
factual_errors.correction: Friction and air resistance are resistive forces. The resultant force is the single combined effect of all the forces acting. Resistive forces slow an object only when they produce a non-zero resultant force opposite to its motion.

factual_errors.text: Correct! Constant velocity means zero acceleration.
factual_errors.correction: The question states only 'constant speed on a level road', not constant velocity. Constant speed with a change of direction (for example on a bend) needs a non-zero resultant force. The question should say the car travels in a straight line.

checkpoint_mismatch.key_point: keyPoints[0]: "an object stays at rest, or keeps moving in a straight line at constant speed"
checkpoint_mismatch.why: The key point requires straight-line motion for zero resultant force. The question gives only 'constant speed' and does not specify a straight path. The answer and feedback therefore treat constant speed as constant velocity, which the key point does not support.
